name: Freshline — the age of your build, on one timeline
one_liner: Drop your package-lock.json into a web page and Freshline draws every dependency version in your build on one time axis — with a red "hot zone" for anything published in the last 7 days, the exact packages that would be blocked by a cooldown, the one-line .npmrc fix, and a shareable "build age" card you can re-run after every install.
problem: Dependency cooldowns (min-release-age) went from a niche recommendation to an ecosystem default in 2026: npm, pnpm, Renovate and Dependabot all shipped it after the npm supply-chain attacks, and analyses found most attacks had a window of opportunity under a week (nesbitt.io). But developers have no fast way to answer the only question that matters before they type `npm ci`: "how much of what I'm about to install is brand new code from the internet?" Today they either install a CLI (npm-cooldown, dep-cooldown), read a wall of text output, or do nothing — which is what almost everyone does. Freshline turns the lockfile they already have into one picture in five seconds, in the browser, with nothing installed and nothing uploaded.
target_customer: JS/TS developers and small teams who ship with npm/pnpm — the crowd that reposts Jack Cable-style security guides, hangs out in r/node, r/webdev, Hacker News and X dev threads. The buyer is nobody; it's free and open source. The people who spread it are the same devs who shared the cooldown posts in 2026.
why_now: Dependency cooldowns became an ecosystem default in 2026: npm ≥11.10 ships `min-release-age`, pnpm, Homebrew, VS Code and Renovate all added cooldown settings (https://christian-schneider.net/blog/dependency-cooldowns-supply-chain-defense/, https://docs.renovatebot.com/key-concepts/minimum-release-age/). Tonight's bookmark — Jack Cable's security guide, reposted by Scott Wu (https://x.com/jackhcable/status/2117731409246978489) — explicitly tells teams to "set a package-age delay of at least seven days, pin versions, commit lockfiles." The setting exists; the before/after picture does not. Everything shipped in 2026, so a tool that visualises cooldown exposure was not useful a year ago.
comparables: npm-cooldown (https://github.com/Veliora-pte-ltd/npm-cooldown) and dep-cooldown (https://github.com/OrtaMarco/dep-cooldown) both audit lockfiles for release age — both are CLIs with text/JSON reports, no visual, no card. Socket.dev's free surface is per-package health pages, not a whole-lockfile age view (https://docs.socket.dev/docs/package-search). GitHub secret scanning and Semgrep address other parts of Cable's list. My deep research found no hosted web app that takes a pasted lockfile and returns a publish-date timeline with a 7-day hot zone and a shareable card. Difference: Freshline is zero-install, visual, personal to your repo, and re-runnable after every `npm update`. Builds on the library's "Strangers" idea (same lockfile input) but a different question and audience framing: Strangers counts *humans with push access*, Freshline measures *how new the code is* and maps directly onto the cooldown setting people are being told to adopt — a different output, a different fix, and a reason to return after each install.
market_note: No revenue intent; this is a free OSS trust-builder. Estimate only: the cooldown HN threads (news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46005111, 46032539) and the repeated 2026 npm attacks suggest tens of thousands of JS devs who already know the term. Willingness to pay ≈ zero; willingness to share ≈ high because the output is a scoreable number about their own repo.
risks: A CLI that already does the audit (dep-cooldown) could add a hosted UI in a weekend. The npm registry could rate-limit or break CORS on heavy client-side fanout, forcing a backend and a hosting bill. Freshness is a proxy, not a verdict: a 2-day-old patch of a well-run package is usually fine, and if the tool cries wolf, devs will dismiss it — the copy has to say "this is cooldown exposure, not malware."
riskiest_assumptions: 1) registry.npmjs.org returns readable CORS responses for a few hundred packument fetches from a static page — the npm registry docs confirm the `time` map exists and browser fetches are generally reported to work, but the CORS header is not officially documented, so a 20-line Cloudflare Worker proxy may be needed (cheap, but it stops it being purely static). 2) Devs care enough about "how new is my build" to run it twice — if the number never changes, it's a one-time toy; the post-install re-run and the diff view are what carry it. 3) Big lockfiles (300+ unique packages for a Next.js app) must resolve in under ~10 seconds without hitting npm 429s; needs batching, caching and an honest progress bar.
first_customers: The devs who reposted Jack Cable's security guide and the cooldown threads: post it as a reply in those threads, in r/node and r/webdev showcase threads, Hacker News Show HN (the cooldown posts there hit the front page twice in 2026), and the Renovate/pnpm Discord channels where cooldown settings are discussed.
validation_test: Post one screenshot of a real, recognisable repo's Freshline timeline (e.g. a fresh create-next-app) with the headline "a 7-day cooldown would have blocked N of your 412 packages" and a waitlist-free link to a static mock. Pass: 50+ people paste their own lockfile within 48 hours, or 10+ reply with their own number. Fail: people like the picture but nobody reports their own number — that means it's a chart, not a tool.
build_plan: Stack: single static page (TypeScript + vanilla or Preact, D3 or hand-rolled SVG), no auth, no DB, deployed on Vercel/Cloudflare Pages; optional 20-line Cloudflare Worker that proxies + caches registry.npmjs.org if CORS or 429s bite. Data: npm packument `time` map (https://registry.npmjs.org/<pkg>) for each resolved version's publish date; `maintainers` and `dist.attestations` for a secondary "unsigned + brand new" flag. Steps: (1) parse package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml client-side, extract name@resolved-version pairs, dedupe; (2) fetch packuments with concurrency ~8, localStorage cache keyed name@version (publish dates never change), progress bar; (3) render the timeline — x-axis = publish date (log-ish scale, today on the right), one dot per package sized by direct/transitive, red hot zone for <7 days, amber <30; (4) the headline numbers: "Build age: median 9 months. 6 packages younger than 7 days. A 7-day cooldown would have blocked 6 of your 412" plus the exact `min-release-age=7d` snippet and the list; (5) shareable PNG card rendered on canvas + "Run again after your next install" that stores the last run in localStorage and shows the diff (new packages that entered the hot zone since last time). Cut for v1: pnpm/yarn/bun lockfiles (npm only), PyPI, vulnerability data, provenance verification, accounts, any server-side storage.
launch_post:
Everyone says "set a 7-day dependency cooldown." Nobody shows you what that would actually block.

Drop your package-lock.json in Freshline: every dependency on one timeline, a red zone for anything published this week, and the exact .npmrc line to fix it.

Runs in your browser. Nothing uploaded.
reasoning: Freshline beat the others because it is the only candidate where a real 2026 behaviour change (cooldowns becoming default across npm, pnpm, Renovate and VS Code) has created a question people are being told to care about — "how new is the code I'm installing?" — with no visual answer anywhere, and where the data to answer it is free, keyless and already in a file the user has open. The teardown, Cuttlefish and follower-growth candidates all died on the same rock: the thing in the bookmark already exists and is better than anything I could ship in a weekend. The secret-scanning and vibe-security candidates died on crowding. It fits the taste file's shape exactly: one input box, no signup, a result in seconds, open source, and a launch post that is mostly the screenshot. It does not overlap tonight's venture (Sidecar serves CNC job-shop estimators chasing vendor quotes; Freshline serves JS developers and shares no audience, workflow or theme). It builds on the library's "Strangers" (same lockfile input) but asks a different question with a different output and a different fix, and it must not reuse that name. could_grow is true but weakly: the honest path to a business is a CI check and an org dashboard for cooldown policy compliance, which is squarely Socket/Semgrep territory — so treat it as a free tool first. Score 7.8, dig_deeper: strong, but usefulness is capped at 7 until someone actually re-runs it twice, and shareability at 8 because I found no viral precedent for this specific output.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Sidecar — outside-processing quote-desk agent for job shops (PICK). Buyer-side of a lane two funded companies left open; cheapest path to a paid pilot.
2. AI quote desk sold to metal finishers themselves — FINALIST, then reshaped into Sidecar. Dropped as a standalone: Forgepoint ($9.8M, Oct 2026) and Steelhead ($84M, 250+ shops) already sell this exact workflow to this exact buyer.
3. DFM pre-flight for hardware-startup engineers (from @hemanthug/twentyfour26) — FINALIST. Dropped: Xometry, Protolabs, Fictiv and Hubs all bundle automated DFM into free instant quoting; no one pays for a standalone checker, and the buyer is an engineer with no budget line.
4. Multi-shop RFQ broadcaster for hardware-startup buyers — dropped at screen. AuraVMS at $4.99/user/mo, oboloo and Axya already cover the generic workflow; the price ceiling is near zero and it is adjacent to the past idea Promiseline.
5. Dev-laptop AI extension/MCP/skill inventory for mid-market (from @ScottWu46 + Jack Cable's guide) — dropped at screen as a near-repeat of past ideas SkillProof and SkillPeek, and killed on gap: StepSecurity Dev Machine Guard already ships this at a published $8/device/month, with Pillar ($9M) and Backslash ($27M) above it.
6. Mobile approval inbox for non-developer agents, across Zapier/UiPath/n8n (from @digitalocean Cuttlefish) — dropped at screen. Strong fit for the builder's UiPath skills, but it is a feature every agent platform ships natively, approval fatigue is the complaint rather than approval access, and it overlaps past ideas Ledger and Doublecheck.
7. "Plaid for government benefits" document-verification wedge for nonprofit benefits navigators (YC RFS, Gustaf Alströmer) — dropped at screen. CivicReach and incumbent case-management vendors already sit in the lane; the real buyer is a state agency with an 18-month procurement cycle, which fails the weeks-to-first-sale test for a nights-and-weekends founder.
8. AI plan-review wedge for city building departments (YC RFS "AI for City Hall") — dropped at screen. Archistar, Symbium and others already sell AI plan review to cities; also a close neighbour of the past idea Backcheck, and city sales cycles are brutal.
9. Governance/inventory for vibe-coded internal apps at SMBs (from @cursor_ai's deploy-from-Cursor launch) — dropped at screen. Superblocks and Caspio are already loudly positioned on "vibe coding sprawl", and the buyer (SMB IT) has latent pain and no budget line yet.
10. Compliance review for AI-drafted client communications at small RIAs — dropped at screen. Hadrius, Comply and Sedric all sell RIA comms surveillance with AI-content coverage; crowded, and far from the builder's domain.
11. "Cognitive debt" review gate for agent-written PRs (from @addyosmani) — dropped at screen. A philosophy, not a purchase order: no named buyer with a budget line, and it is thin variation on the past idea EvalSeed.

PROJECT
1. Freshline — lockfile → publish-date timeline + 7-day hot zone + cooldown card. PICK: real 2026 behaviour change (cooldowns everywhere), free keyless data, visual output, reason to return after each install.
2. Teardown-in-the-browser — photo of an object → interactive exploded 3D. Dropped at screen: the bookmark's own skill (elvarofficial/teardown, ~2.2k stars) already owns this, image-to-3D APIs cost $0.20-0.50/gen, and "Exploded" is already in the library.
3. Cognitive Debt Report — paste a Claude/Cursor transcript, get a score for how much you accepted unverified. Dropped at screen: no honest way to measure it, output is a lecture nobody posts, and it sails close to Addy Osmani's article rather than adding to it.
4. Mess Map — repo URL → visual map of copy-paste, dead wrappers, leaky abstractions (from /untangle-codebase). Dropped at screen: jscpd and GitDiagram cover the halves for free, and "untangle" is already a shipped product in the bookmark.
5. Secretsweep — browser-side scan of a dropped folder for leaked keys. Dropped at screen: gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning and a dozen free SaaS already do it; nothing left to add in a weekend.
6. Agent Approval Inbox — a shareable mock of "approve this migration from your phone" (from DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish). Dropped at screen: it's their product, and a demo with no agent behind it is a fake.
7. Startup Follower Race — animated 90-day X follower growth chart for startups (from @benln). Dropped at screen: no public dataset or affordable X API for historical follower counts; I would have to fabricate the data.
8. MCP/Extension Shelf — audit your installed editor extensions and MCP servers. Dropped at screen: mcp-audit, mcp-config-audit and coding-agent-audit already exist as free CLIs, and a browser page cannot read local config without the user hand-picking files.
9. Vibe-Ship Check — scan a deployed URL for exposed keys and missing RLS. Finalist, then dropped: VibeEval's Vibe Code Scanner, CheckVibe and VibeDoctor already sell exactly this, and an honest scan needs a backend.
10. Launch Lag — track how long between "describe the tool" and a live shared link, from the Cursor live-apps bookmark. Dropped at screen: nothing to measure, no data source, no output worth posting.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish (confirmed it is a mobile approve/deny console for coding agents, which killed candidate 6 as a feature rather than a product); Jack Cable's security guide (gave the concrete incident list — tampered AI coding-tool installer in the Binance chain, Shai-Hulud worm — and surfaced "inventory editor, browser and AI extensions and MCP servers" as the recommended action, which seeded candidate 5); Addy Osmani's "Critical thinking when agents do the work" (confirmed it is an essay about cognitive surrender, not a product gap — candidate 11 died here). I could not see the images or videos in any bookmark and did not guess at them.

Screening pot (6/6): one call each on dev-machine AI inventory (StepSecurity at $8/device/mo already sells it — candidate 5 dead), benefits-navigator software (CivicReach exists; buyer is a state agency — candidate 7 dead), vibe-coded internal-app governance (Superblocks owns the positioning — candidate 9 dead), machine-shop quoting (found Paperless Parts, Uptool, CloudNC, Dashnode — kept as finalist), mobile agent approvals (no cross-platform product, but approval fatigue is the complaint not approval access — candidate 6 dead), RIA AI-comms compliance (Hadrius/Comply/Sedric — candidate 10 dead).

Deep research pot (12/12): on the two surviving finalists. Pulled pricing and funding for Paperless Parts (quote-only; vendor says third-party price listings are wrong), Uptool ($195/mo, $6M seed Feb 2026), CloudNC Quote Agent ($20/mo starter), Steelhead ($84M from Mainsail, 250+ shops), Anoplex ($150/$125/$375 per month tiers), Forgepoint/Frank ($9.8M seed Oct 2026, Primary + a16z speedrun, seven-figure ARR claimed). Chased quoting benchmarks and found the honest state: a 20-35% win rate on submitted quotes and 3.8-4.5 day quote turnaround exist as vendor-published benchmarks with no survey behind them, so I did not lean on them. Checked the DFM/marketplace side (Xometry, Protolabs, Fictiv, Hubs all bundle free automated DFM) which killed candidate 3. Checked buyer-side RFQ tools (AuraVMS, oboloo, Axya, Precoro) which killed candidate 4 and simultaneously showed none of them read prints or handle spec flowdown — the first hint of the real gap. Checked finisher-side industry structure (~5,000 establishments, two-thirds under 20 employees) and finisher job postings (estimator/inside-sales roles at Aberfoyle Metal Treaters and Advanced Plating Technologies that explicitly list "follow up with customers for missing information"), which confirmed the manual loop exists on both ends.

Sharpening pot (5/5): two calls to test flipping from the finisher to the machine shop — one on whether anyone serves buyer-side OSP (nobody does end-to-end; ERPs only record a cost a human already fetched), one on Forgepoint specifically (confirmed it serves finishers as sellers, which is the side I vacated). Three calls to test the narrowed wedge: outside-process lead times (2-5 days heat treat, 3-7 plating, 25-100% expedite premiums), whether rate cards are standing or per-job (per-job for anything non-routine; finishers do not publish customer-facing schedules), and whether estimators guess (yes — prior quotes and provisional estimates, with lot minimums, rack charges and freight the named failure modes). What changed because of the pots: the idea moved from the wrong side of the transaction to the right one, and from a vague "manage outside processing" scope to the single pre-award moment where money is actually lost.

Investor signals weighed: YC W27 "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (the closest fit — this agent turns an office person into a spec-flowdown specialist), "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" (both generated candidates, both died on procurement cycle length and existing incumbents); a16z Big Ideas 2026 "The renaissance of the American factory", "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" and "Systems of record lose ground" (all three support the thesis that the value is in small industrial back offices, not in a new ERP). I deliberately did not propose any signal as the idea itself.
Sharpening (7 to 8.1): Round 1 — weak criterion: gap (6.5). The first shape was a generic "AI quote desk for metal finishing shops", i.e. sell to the finisher. Two sharpening calls killed it: Forgepoint's "Frank" (forgepoint.ai/industries/metal-finishing) is explicitly aimed at coating and heat-treat shops, raised $9.8M in Oct 2026 from Primary + a16z speedrun, reports seven-figure ARR within six months, and already extracts masking, testing and spec requirements; Steelhead has $84M from Mainsail and 250+ finishing shops with quoting built in. That gap is closed by funded players serving the same buyer with the same workflow. Change to the idea: flip sides of the transaction — sell to the machine shop *buying* outside processing, not the finisher selling it. Research then confirmed the buyer side is bare: a dedicated call on buyer-side OSP found no platform that sends one spec-correct package to multiple processors and returns comparable quotes; ERPs (Bizowie, JobPack, netray worksheets) only record a subcontract cost a human already obtained. gap 6.5 → 8.0, and market_pull 7 → 8 because the machine shop buyer has a documented software budget ($195-$750/mo precedents) and is the same persona Uptool and Paperless Parts already sell to.

Round 2 — weak criterion: pain (6.5, thin on numbers). Change: narrowed the wedge from "manage outside processing" to the single most expensive moment — the unconfirmed OSP price at quote time. Two calls tested whether that moment is real and costly. Found: trade sources name waiting on outside-process prices as the explicit bottleneck against a 24-48h quote target; heat treat is quoted at 2-5 days turnaround and plating 3-7 (one source: 5-14 business days door-to-door with expedite surcharges of 25-100%); shops do fall back to prior quotes or provisional estimates and the named failure modes are missed lot minimums, rack/setup charges and freight; OSP appears in an estimated 30-40% of jobs at many shops. What I did NOT find, and am not claiming: any survey quantifying margin lost to stale OSP prices, or OSP spend as a share of COGS. So pain goes 6.5 → 7.5, not higher: the mechanism is confirmed by multiple trade sources and the workaround (guessing, chasing by email) is documented, but no hard dollar figure exists, which is exactly what the validation test is designed to produce.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised Addy Osmani's "cognitive debt" article, Jack Cable's security guide (which produced the cooldown thread that became the pick), and the elvar teardown skill — the last one killed candidate 2 by showing the skill is already open source with ~2.2k stars. Screening pot (5/5): one check each on cooldown tooling, secret scanners, teardown/image-to-3D prior art, cognitive-debt tooling, and the X follower dataset — killed candidates 2, 3, 5, 7. Deep pot (8/8): confirmed npm-cooldown and dep-cooldown are CLIs only; confirmed Socket.dev's free web surface does not give a whole-lockfile age view; confirmed registry.npmjs.org packuments carry a per-version `time` map with no API key; confirmed download/metadata rate limits and that CORS is reported-working but not officially documented (which is why buildability is 8, not 9, and why the plan includes a fallback Worker); confirmed a Next.js lockfile is commonly 300+ unique packages, which set the batching/caching design; checked the Mess Map and vibe-ship-check finalists and found both crowded. Sharpen pot (4/4): searched specifically for a hosted lockfile freshness timeline with a shareable card (none found), for a viral precedent (none found — this is why shareability is 8 not 9), checked provenance/attestation fields as a secondary signal, and re-verified the cooldown ecosystem shipping dates. What changed: the idea moved from "another dependency audit" to "the picture of your build's age plus the exact blocked list," and gained the post-install diff.
Sharpening (7.2 to 7.8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you look at your timeline once and close the tab). Change: added the post-install re-run loop — Freshline stores your last run in localStorage and on the next visit shows the diff ("3 packages entered the hot zone since Tuesday"), plus the explicit "would a 7-day cooldown have blocked these?" count that changes every time you update. Research (deep pot: perplexity on dep-cooldown/npm-cooldown and Socket.dev free surface) confirmed the existing tools are CLIs with one-shot text reports and no stored history or diff, so the returning-user angle is unclaimed. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped at 7: I have no evidence devs actually re-run it; the loop is plausible, not proven). Score 6.6 → 7.2.
Round 2 — weak criteria: shareability and wow (both 7: a dependency audit is not inherently postable). Change: made the output a picture rather than a list — every package as a dot on one publish-date time axis with a red last-7-days zone, and the headline framed as a personal number about *your* repo ("a 7-day cooldown would have blocked 6 of your 412"), rendered to a PNG card. Research (sharpen pot: searched for an existing hosted lockfile freshness timeline / shareable card, and checked that registry packuments carry a per-version `time` map fetchable client-side) found no hosted web app doing this and confirmed the data exists for free with no key. Wow 7 → 8, shareability 7 → 8, buildability 7 → 8 (dependency confirmed real, free, no auth; CORS still the one unknown, which is why it is 8 and not 9). Score 7.2 → 7.8.
prototype_summary: Freshline is a browser-only prototype that turns a lockfile into a single timeline showing how freshly published every dependency is, flags the 5 packages a 7-day cooldown would block, and hands over the one-line .npmrc fix plus a shareable card.
